title: Commentary: Can Nebraska learn from Kansas’ mistakes?
description: We Nebraskans had better learn from what happened in Kansas under Gov. Sam Brownback and a state legislature dominated by Republican politicians beginning just 14 short years ago. And we better do it quick. In 2012, Brownback and the Kansas Legislature enacted significant tax cuts that soon produced unsustainable revenue shortfalls, budget deficits, credit r[...]
text:
A budget book for Nebraska's fiscal years between 2025 and 2027 sits on a lawmaker's desk. April 29, 2025. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)We Nebraskans had better learn from what happened in Kansas under Gov. Sam Brownback and a state legislature dominated by Republican politicians beginning just 14 short years ago. And we better do it quick.
In 2012, Brownback and the Kansas Legislature enacted significant tax cuts that soon produced unsustainable revenue shortfalls, budget deficits, credit rating downgrades and deep cuts to vital governmental services like public education and roads. Is any of this sounding familiar? 
In 2012, legislation was passed that cut Kansas’ top state personal income tax rate from 6.45% to 4.9%. That was done so Kansas could “compete” with neighboring states with lower state income tax rates. The same law eliminated state income taxes on pass-through entities, prompting the creation of hundreds of thousands of small businesses that paid their owners pass-through “profits” rather than “wages,” allowing them to pay zero state income tax on those earnings. 
Kansas’ revenue dropped $700 million in the first year alone. Ultimately, the state Supreme Court ordered the state to increase state funding of public K-12 education in 2017 and 2018 by $293 million in order to meet the state constitutional requirement that the state provide public education. Is any of this sounding familiar? 
Brownback and his Republican cronies insisted that the tax cuts would pay for themselves through an explosion of economic growth. That did not happen, to put it mildly. 
Instead, the Kansas economy grew at near average annual rates, and the loss of revenue from the tax cuts produced multimillion-dollar budgetary deficits and deep cuts to needed services like those to public education that the Supreme Court’s order attempted to remedy. Brownback’s approval rating fell to 25%, and Republicans lost seats in the Kansas Legislature in the 2016 election that elevated Donald Trump to the White House. In 2017, the Kansas Legislature repealed the 2012 tax cuts over Brownback’s veto. 
Here in Nebraska, the state budget was bulging with a $1 billion surplus in 2021 and 2022, largely from receipt of one-time federal relief dollars in the wake of the COVID economic downturn. That surplus was offered as rationale for cutting the state income tax rate so Nebraska could “compete” with lower-taxing neighboring states. 
In 2023, Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed into law LB 754, passed by a Republican-dominated Unicameral that implemented, starting for the 2024 tax year, a phased-in reduction of the state income tax rate from 6.84% to 3.99% for the 2027 tax year. Ever since, we here in the Cornhusker State have watched our governor and state legislators scramble to repeatedly fill hundreds-of-millions-of-dollars holes in the state’s budget — holes caused by the reduction in revenue resulting from the income tax rate cuts.
Pillen directed state agencies to implement across-the-board spending cuts of 8%. Money was pulled from specifically designated funds such as the State Veterans Aid Fund, which provides for the needs of our state’s citizens who served in our nation’s armed forces, and the Environmental Trust, the funding for which is a portion of state lottery revenues as voters mandated when the lottery was approved by them in 1992. The clamber goes on to patch a deficit of approximately $300 million in the current budget, and projections are for a $1.2 billion deficit for the next two-year state budget that senators will be confronted with in the upcoming session. 
In our Big Red state, registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats by at least 20 percentage points. After being reelected two weeks ago by a margin of 7% over Democrat candidate Lynn Walz, Republican Gov. Pillen claimed a “mandate” for his policy of tax cuts and spending reductions, the policies that have produced the deficits, directives for cuts and raids on state funds. 
Pillen insists that his approach of capping local government spending, the state paying the operational expenses of public education and cutting property taxes is the “fix” voters demand. Noticeably, Pillen fails to explain where the state — which has already exhausted the underside of every couch cushion to pay past bills and is still facing a $1.2 billion shortfall in the next biennial budget — is going to come up with anything near the $3.3 billion in local property taxes spent annually on public education.  
Perhaps we can learn Kansas’ lesson? If the economic and societal damage sustained by our neighbors to the south is insufficient disincentive for following the path Pillen advocates, maybe the loss of elective office by the Kansas politicians who went along with an irresponsible fiscal fantasy will be.

description: The North Slope Borough sued the state of Alaska on Thursday, seeking to halt a proposed petroleum property tax change that could slash local tax revenue by more than 70%, leaving the North Slope unable to pay debts, operate schools and fund basic services. “A reduction of this magnitude would have devastating consequences for North […]
text:
ConocoPhillips' CD-5 drill site is one of the existing extensions to the company's major Alpine development on Alaska's North Slope. A new Alpine extension, CD-8, is provoking objections because of its proposed location: two miles from the Iñupiaq village of Nuiqsut. (ConocoPhillips)The North Slope Borough sued the state of Alaska on Thursday, seeking to halt a proposed petroleum property tax change that could slash local tax revenue by more than 70%, leaving the North Slope unable to pay debts, operate schools and fund basic services.
“A reduction of this magnitude would have devastating consequences for North Slope communities and severely impair the borough’s ability to sustain essential services and government operations,” borough attorneys wrote in a request for a preliminary injunction that would bar the state from making the change in the immediate future. 
The suit, filed in Anchorage Superior Court and assigned to Judge Yvonne Lamoureux, names the governor, lieutenant governor and other officials as defendants.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The state’s proposed change would affect local governments across Alaska and the state itself. Under state law, Alaska charges a 2% tax on qualifying oil and gas property, and local governments may take custody of some or all of the revenue generated from property within their borders. 
In a public notice Oct. 29, the Alaska Department of Revenue said it is planning to significantly increase a tax deduction for “intangible drilling expenses,” netting oil and gas companies a significantly smaller tax bill.
“I am concerned that the proposed methodology could place more than 70% of the Borough’s assessed property tax base at risk,” wrote the North Slope Borough’s finance director, Fadil Limani, in an affidavit submitted with the borough’s legal complaint.
On the North Slope, that tax accounts for the vast majority of local government revenue. While the Alaska Municipal League and the Kenai Peninsula Borough have submitted public comments against the proposed change, only the North Slope Borough is thus far named as a plaintiff.
Unusually, the state did not notify local governments or state legislators about the proposed tax change until Nov. 10, more than a week after the public notice was published. 
“As the representative of communities directly affected by North Slope oil and gas property taxation, I should not have to learn of a consequential proposed change through others rather than through the formal notice process established by the Legislature,” wrote Rep. Robyn Niayuq Frier, D-Utqiagvik, in a public comment requesting the state to halt the regulation change.    

Rep. Robyn Niayuq Frier, D-Utqiagvik, speaks on the House floor on the last day of the regular legislative session on May 20, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

The proposed regulation change wasn’t signed by the director of the department’s tax division but by a political appointee, Deputy Commissioner Lee Cruise.
The reason for the change, listed by the state in an appendix, is to “streamline regulatory ambiguity” under an administrative order issued by Gov. Mike Dunleavy in August 2025.
In its request for preliminary injunction, the North Slope Borough suggests a different motive.
For years, the state and Oil Search Alaska LLC have been fighting a legal dispute over the proper value of that company’s oil and gas property on the North Slope.
This year, the Alaska Department of Revenue estimated the taxable value of Oil Search’s relevant Pikka Project property at $52.6 million for 2024, $128.5 million for 2025, and $197.8 million according to the North Slope Borough’s legal complaint.
Oil Search has said the taxable value should instead be $2 million, $7 million, and $1.9 million respectively, according to the North Slope Borough, according to the complaint.
Those values are almost identical to what would be collected if the new tax exemptions become final.
In its request for a preliminary injunction, the North Slope Borough says that “the new regulations appear to be the result of lobbying efforts by Oil Search based on the identical language in the proposed regulation and Oil Search’s internal documents.”
Under the standard regulatory timeline, the state’s proposed change would take effect Dec. 30, immediately before taxes are assessed on Jan. 1.
For that reason, the borough said in its filings, it is requesting a speedy hearing on the issue.
No court date had been set by the end of Friday.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC school districts receive $311 million in grants as facility needs climb to $18 billion
description: Seven North Carolina school districts will receive nearly $311 million in state grants for school construction and renovation projects, the state Department of Public Instruction announced this week.  NCDPI said it received 77 applications from 46 districts, requesting nearly $2 billion in total. The money comes from a lottery-funded program created by the G[...]
text:
This week the State Board of Education released a new report that detailed $18 billion in school facility needs over the next five years for the state’s 115 school systems. (Image: Adobe Stock)Seven North Carolina school districts will receive nearly $311 million in state grants for school construction and renovation projects, the state Department of Public Instruction announced this week. 
NCDPI said it received 77 applications from 46 districts, requesting nearly $2 billion in total. The money comes from a lottery-funded program created by the General Assembly in 2017. 
“These grants will help districts better serve students, educators and communities with healthy, safe and secure learning environments that enhance the overall quality of education across the state,” State Superintendent Maurice “Mo” Green said in a statement.
The largest award, $62 million, will go to Elizabeth City-Pasquotank Public Schools to renovate Northeastern High School, which serves students in grades six through 12. The project also includes a career and technical education center serving the district. 
Lee County Schools will receive $52 million to merge two existing campuses into a new middle school that includes a districtwide career and technical education center. 
Another four districts will each receive $42 million each to build new elementary school schools, the cap for elementary school projects. 
North Carolina school facility funding needs climb 37% to nearly $18 billion

The grants come as North Carolina school districts see a big jump in facility needs and face questions about how to pay for them, especially with a newly passed constitutional amendment on property tax limits that threatens a key way counties raise money for schools. Public schools have nearly $18 billion in projected facility needs over the next five years, a 37% increase from the 2020-21 assessment, according to a DPI survey released earlier this month. 
The report also estimates another $14.78 billion in needs for years six through 10, which brings the total projected needs over the coming decade to nearly $33 billion. Much of that spending, $9.8 billion, is for renovations, a 77% increase from the previous survey. About $6.2 billion will be needed to build new schools.
Among the seven districts receiving grants, Hoke County Schools reported the largest five-year facility needs, at about $283 million, but received a $42 million award which will go towards building a new elementary school. It’s a fraction of what’s needed, but a spokesperson said it’s a welcome relief in a district where four of the eight elementary schools were built between 1945 and 1957. 
“While this funding addresses a significant priority, substantial needs remain across the school system, including classroom additions, renovations, and improvements to mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and other building systems,” a district spokesperson said.
Bertie County Schools, which reported about $41 million in facility repair needs, received a $42 million grant for a new elementary school. A district spokesperson said it will not address needs at Bertie Early College, Bertie High School or Bertie Middle School.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Task force dives into possible changes to Kansas school funding as current formula is set to expire
description: TOPEKA — A legislative committee resumed the challenging task this week of examining possible new school funding models to replace the one the state was forced to use by the courts.  Since 2016, the state has used a formula set after the settlement of a lawsuit that challenged the state for not fully funding education, […]
text:
Leah Fliter, assistant executive director of advocacy for the Kansas Association of School Boards, shown here testifyign in February, watched the Education Funding Task Force  with interest to track how possible changes to the public school funding formula would affect school districts statewide. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Legislature video)TOPEKA — A legislative committee resumed the challenging task this week of examining possible new school funding models to replace the one the state was forced to use by the courts. 
Since 2016, the state has used a formula set after the settlement of a lawsuit that challenged the state for not fully funding education, said Leah Fliter, lobbyist at Kansas Association of School Boards.
With legislation that adopted the formula set to expire June 30, 2027, lawmakers are looking at how they can adjust the formula. 
The Education Funding Task Force considered more than 15 models with a variety of scenarios at its Tuesday and Wednesday meetings. Discussions ranged from pulling gifted education from special education funding to its own category to how weightings could be changed to support better literacy education in kindergarten through third grades.
Fliter said she watched the proceedings with interest to make sure the Legislature continues to fund at the current level. 
Task force members haven’t shown interest in cutting school funding overall, but the many models they considered would affect funding by school district whenever the formula changes, she said. Each district has different mixes of students with different needs. 
“Whenever you tweak the formula, you do end up with districts that gain money and districts that potentially lose money, so a winners-and-losers thing that plays out when you start to push and pull the levers and the buttons in the school formula,” she said. 
The “levers” are pieces of the funding formula that support services like special education, at-risk students and high or low enrollments. Each student gets base state aid and then, depending on extra needs, additional monies, Fliter said. 
“The formula was built to have these different weightings in place to to help make sure that everybody is getting an equitable and adequate education, regardless of where they live in the state,” Fliter said. 
The concept of whether a formula might lower or raise the amount school districts receive was one that caused disagreement within the task force. Rep. Nikki McDonald, D-Olathe, said she couldn’t foresee accepting a formula that gave any school districts fewer dollars than what they currently receive. 
Sen. Renee Erickson, R-Wichita, said any changes to the formula were certain to affect districts in a variety of ways. 
“The reality is that when we start making any change, no district is probably going to get exactly the same amount,” she said. “If that’s our goal, give everybody the same amount, then we just wasted two years of talking about what are some changes we can do better on the school finance formula.”
The current funding formula already has its own challenges, including how it accounts for inflation, Fliter said. Lawmakers in 2019 satisfied the Kansas Supreme Court by agreeing to automatically increase funding each year by the average increase in the Midwest consumer price index for the past three years.
“It was developed under a set of factors that really are no longer true,” she said. “They were not taking into account that inflation was going to do what it did, especially around the COVID pandemic.”
The inflationary adjustment doesn’t account for the actual increases in personnel costs, such as insurance and other benefits, Fliter said. 
The task force is scheduled to meet again in December.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: School funding reform could prompt constitutional convention, Greenwald says
description: Voters should approve eventual school funding reforms, the Assembly Majority Leader suggested during a panel discussion Wednesday.
text:
Assemblyman Lou Greenwald (D-Camden), pictured with Assemblywoman Eliana Pintor Marin (D-Essex), speaks about the $50.6 billion budget New Jersey lawmakers approved on June 29, 2022. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey should call a constitutional convention to include voters in the approval of a new school funding formula once a proposal is finalized, Assembly Majority Leader Lou Greenwald (D-Camden) said.
Though legislators and Gov. Mikie Sherrill in August began soliciting input for changes to the state’s funding formula, officials have said little about how their eventual proposal would differ from the funding formula enacted in 2008, and it’s not clear whether or how a formula enshrined in the state’s constitution would affect court precedent that demands New Jersey students receive a thorough and efficient education.
“I think ultimately this is going to need to lead to a constitutional convention and then a question that will include the voters as part of the solution because I think, ultimately at the end of the day, this is an issue that New Jersey has struggled with for generations,” Greenwald said Wednesday during a panel discussion at the New Jersey League of Municipalities’ annual conference.
In New Jersey, the state calculates how much each municipality must spend to provide their students a constitutionally sound education and how much those districts can raise on their own based on their residents’ incomes and property values.
State aid fills the rest, though not all districts raise enough revenue to meet the local spending — called a local fair share — needed to fully fund schools after state aid is added.
Some cannot raise enough revenue locally because of the state’s 2% cap on annual property tax levies, and others have been hammered by steep swings in state aid as the state in 2018 moved to begin phasing out aid meant to keep districts whole after the enactment of the 2008 funding formula.
At present, local governments in New Jersey look to property taxes to fund their share of school expenses, and Greenwald suggested that could change as a result of the yet-to-be-determined reforms.
“We need to understand that we are fixing a fundamentally broken tax system that dates back to the origins of this state as one of the founding states of this country,” Greenwald said.
New Jersey in 2024 tied with Illinois for the highest property tax rate in the nation, according to the Tax Foundation, and the average property tax bill in the state rose to a record high $10,570 last year.
It’s unclear what changes to the state’s funding formula lawmakers will eventually propose. The Department of Education last week said it would continue soliciting feedback from stakeholders at least through December.
Senate Majority Leader Teresa Ruiz (D-Essex) earlier told the Monitor she does not expect a proposal to be ready before the end of the current July-to-June fiscal year.
Among some other things, the reforms aim to better fund school transportation and extraordinary special education.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Data centers, teacher pay part of West Virginia Treasurer’s agenda
description: The West Virginia State Treasurer announced a packed agenda for the 2027 legislative session, saying he’ll be advocating teacher raises and reform to the data center law.
text:
West Virginia Treasurer Larry Pack, standing in front of the Treasurer Office’s vault, tells reporters about his agenda for the 2027 legislative session on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Photo by Henry Culvyhouse/West Virginia Watch)The West Virginia State Treasurer announced a packed agenda for the 2027 legislative session, saying he’ll be advocating teacher raises and reform to the data center law. 
Standing in front of the office’s vault, Treasurer Larry Pack said data center law, known by its bill number House Bill 2014, and education were top concerns he heard from residents across the state. 
“I’m just amazed that people know a House bill number and what it’s about,” Pack said. “That speaks to the controversy, that speaks to the magnitude of the bill that was passed a couple years ago.” 
Pack said he’ll be working with the Legislature to introduce legislation to reset how taxes are allocated, keeping property taxes for county commissions and school boards like any other economic development project. 
Pack said he had concerns that school districts weren’t getting a dime for data centers, because the current formulation sends most of the money to the state to be placed in an income tax reduction fund. 
“The money when it first comes in, goes in an account called personal income tax refunds,” Pack said. “ But before the year end is out, it’s just transferred to the general fund.” 
“But there’s nothing in 2014 that talks about a tax cut,” he continued. “There’s nothing in there that gives a tax cut to West Virginians in 2014. The money, the money when it first comes in, goes in an account called personal income tax refunds. But before the year end is out, it’s just transferred to the general fund.”
While Pack’s data center plan is focused on property taxation, he said he’s supportive of looking into wider reforms on data centers in West Virginia. 
“Data centers are bringing amazing opportunities to West Virginia in terms of jobs. In terms of investment, in terms of being able to use the fossil fuels and the oil and gas that we create in West Virginia,” Pack said. 
“But there’s no question that I believe there needs to be more transparency. There needs to be local input,” he said. “But we’re trying to just focus on the dollar portion of it.” 
For teachers, Pack said he’s pushing for a $50,000 floor for all teachers in the state and a $2,000 raise for those above the threshold. Pack also called for elimination of the “grid” — a matrix contained in state law that outlines the pay for teachers for each year of service. 
“We got to give local control. We have more ability to do what they want to do,” Pack said. 
However, under questioning from Bob Aaron, of WCHS, Pack didn’t really call for a locality pay structure for areas of the state like the Eastern Panhandle, which has long been hemorrhaging teachers to Virginia and Maryland for higher wages. 
“I think we need to come up with a system where every board, every county board of education can have their own pay scale,” Pack said. 
Other proposals from Pack include: 

A constitutional amendment to put a three-term limit on elected members of the Board of Public Works, which would include Pack’s office, the state auditor, the agricultural commissioner, the attorney general and the secretary of state. 
A constitutional amendment to eliminate the business inventory tax. Pack said this would cost the state $100 million and is different from the elimination of personal property business tax that voters rejected in 2022.  
Changing appointments to boards, which he said numbered around 100 throughout the state and are all appointed by the governor.  Pack said he would like to see around 10 boards be appointed by members of the wider Board of Public Works to offload that responsibility.
Sunset on tax credits. Pack said tax credits should be up for renewal by the Legislature every five years. 
Reform of unclaimed property. Pack said he wants to see the laws tightened to make sure the rightful owners of unclaimed property being held at the Treasurer’s Office can be returned.
